title: The Roaring Twenties and Prohibition
objective: After this level you can explain what changed in the 1920s, and why Americans banned alcohol in 1920 and repealed the ban in 1933.
summary: In a newly urban nation, temperance reformers won national Prohibition in 1920; bootlegging, crime and the Depression, plus a women's repeal movement, ended it in 1933.

cards.headline: In 1920 the US banned alcohol. In 1933 it changed its mind.
cards.body: Why would a nation amend its Constitution to stop people drinking, then amend it again to undo the ban?

cards.headline: A new kind of country
cards.body: The decade opened on a changed nation. The 1920 census was the first in which most Americans lived in urban areas. That same year, Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify the 19th Amendment, completing women's right to vote nationwide. New city crowds and new voters would both shape the fight over drinking.

cards.headline: The dry crusade
cards.body: From the 1870s the Women's Christian Temperance Union saw alcohol as the source of many social ills, including ruined families. Reformers won the 18th Amendment, which banned the "manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors" for drinking. National Prohibition began in January 1920.

cards.headline: Speakeasies and gangsters
cards.body: Illegal liquor stayed easy to find. Gangsters like Al Capone grew rich from bootlegging and bribed police, judges and politicians. The law meant to clean up society had created a booming criminal industry.

cards.headline: Women for repeal
cards.body: In 1929 Pauline Sabin founded the Women's Organization for National Prohibition Reform. Its members argued Prohibition had led to more unregulated and underage drinking and to distrust of the law, and it grew to 1.5 million reported members. After the 1929 crash, the promise of jobs and tax revenue added support. The 21st Amendment, ratified December 5, 1933, repealed the 18th.

cards.headline: The Roaring Twenties and Prohibition: explained
learned: By 1920 most Americans lived in urban areas
Prohibition fed bootlegging and organized crime
Women's groups and the Depression helped win repeal in 1933

questions.prompt: Which amendment ended national Prohibition in 1933?
questions.explanation: The 21st Amendment, ratified December 5, 1933, repealed the 18th.

questions.prompt: Why did support for repealing Prohibition grow by the early 1930s?

options.label: Alcohol had become impossible to find
options.rationale: Illegal liquor stayed easy to find.

options.label: Bootlegging crime spread, and the Depression made jobs and taxes tempting
The Supreme Court struck Prohibition down

questions.explanation: Bootlegging fed crime and corruption, and after the 1929 crash legal alcohol promised jobs and tax revenue.

questions.prompt: Women won the vote nationwide in 1920 (Level 69). What part did women play in the fight over Prohibition?

options.label: They led groups on both sides

questions.explanation: The Women's Christian Temperance Union fought for Prohibition; Pauline Sabin's women's organization fought to repeal it.
